text: A dance contest pays out to the winning couple, and the man collects the whole prize. Mercedes performs in a cabaret because her sister's studies have to be paid for by somebody, and the partner she turns with on the floor is also the person who decides what her work is worth. Emilio Fernández treats the ballroom as a workplace, with shifts, rivals, and a hierarchy that puts Paco above her, so the pressure on Mercedes is never abstract for a second: it is a sum of money, owed and withheld, night after night. The dancing is not relief from the story. It is where the story is transacted. What holds the picture is the doubleness of the floor itself, where two people must look like partners for the length of a number and then settle up once the music stops.

Two bars of chocolate, stolen in April 1945, were enough to get a soldier shot. Rudi got away from the firing squad and has been scraping a living off the street ever since; the judge who signed the sentence stayed exactly where he was and is now a respected public prosecutor. They pass on the street one day. What Dr. Schramm does next is not violence but procedure, an arrest, pressure applied through the police, the ordinary apparatus turned on one peddler so that a private matter stays private. What Rudi did in 1945 was steal food; what he does now is exist within walking distance of a man with a career. Wolfgang Staudte's film is filed as comedy as much as drama, and the comedy is administrative. Fourteen years separate the court-martial from the release date, arithmetic a 1959 audience could do without any help from the screen.

Elena arrives in an unfamiliar city with nothing arranged and nobody behind her, and the first man who is kind to her is working. Her parents' household has come apart; a dinner invitation ends with a drugged glass and a sale, and she wakes as the property of Rosaura, who runs a brothel out of her nightclub. Elena becomes the main attraction on that floor. Alberto Gout keeps three things going at once, the numbers, the criminal economy paying for them, and Elena's own patience, which is exact about names. That third thread is what separates the film from sorrow: she is not enduring anything, she is waiting, and the waiting has a list attached to it. The songs, then, are not intermissions between the unpleasant parts. They are the one piece of the job that everybody is permitted to watch.

A singer stands in one night for a friend who performs as a woman on stage, and the house concludes that she is a man. Susanne's break arrives in the shape of a disguise she cannot afterwards put down: the work is steady only while the mistake holds, and the mistake has to be maintained in every room she enters. Reinhold Schünzel builds the whole comedy out of doubled knowledge, and never once cheats it. The audience inside the theater is confidently wrong, the audience watching the film is not, and the distance between the two is where the laughter comes from. Then the tour reaches London, where a man in the habit of pursuing women starts to notice that something in the act does not add up. Underneath the farce sits a plain employment arrangement, and it lasts exactly as long as the people paying stay fooled.

The plan is to keep a czar so continuously entertained that he never reaches the negotiating table. It belongs to an Austrian prince, and it goes wrong in an instructive direction: the czar hires a man built to his own measurements and sends the copy out to be entertained, which leaves the original free to appear everywhere and answer for nothing. Then both of them want the same woman, and the scheme meets a difficulty that no protocol covers. Erik Charell stages high diplomacy as a staffing problem, and the beautiful women arranged around the czar are part of the same logistics. The comedy is structural rather than verbal, since everything funny in it comes from two men occupying one office, and from a settlement being negotiated by whoever happens to be standing in the room at the time.

Portraits of Huerta and Zapata are both kept at the hacienda, and only one goes up at a time. Mendoza has the walls changed according to who is riding up the road: the government's men find a loyal supporter, the revolutionaries find a friend, and either way there is a party, with drink and courtesy and a table laid. Fernando de Fuentes lets the routine run long enough that it stops being funny, and then lets it run further. The hospitality is genuine, which is precisely the trouble, since a man warm to both sides is soon obliged to both, and eighty-five minutes is exactly enough time for the courtesy to run out of room. The revolution enters this film through the front door, at dinner, in the voice a host uses with guests he cannot afford to disappoint.

Doña Herlinda has decided that her son will be happy, and she owns the house where that is going to occur. He is a doctor. He has a lover, and his mother's response is not objection but accommodation: her own rooms made available, discretion supplied free of charge, and then a marriage of convenience arranged with the same competence. Jaime Humberto Hermosillo films the entire negotiation in furniture and mealtimes, and nobody declares anything, because nobody has to. The son gets everything he wants and none of it on his own terms, which is the small print of the arrangement. The comedy runs on the gap between a family's manners and its actual affairs, held open indefinitely by mutual agreement. Maternal love is an administrative talent here, and it obtains results that candor would never have got near.

The premise fits on one line: a poor man robs the rich and hands it back down his own street. A hundred minutes is a lot of running time for a single sentence of plot, which indicates where the film actually lives, in the rooms and doorways and standing arrangements of a barrio where everybody already knows who he is. Gilberto Martínez Solares spends that time on manner rather than method. What a Robin Hood needs, it turns out, is not nerve but an audience of neighbors. Theft becomes an occupation with regular hours and a clientele, and the block adjusts to having a benefactor much as it would adjust to a new grocer. The Somos hundred keeps it. Nothing in it asks the poor to be noble first in order to have earned the money afterwards.

Someone left a baby in a trash can; the woman who found him kept him. She dances at a nightclub, which is where the difficulty starts, because the work wants her available and unattached and the people around her want much the same thing for reasons of their own. Emilio Fernández never stages the decision as a moral debate. It happens in a moment, and everything after it is the practical business of raising a child inside a life not built to hold one, with acquaintances who grow slower to answer. Mexico, 1950. The child is not a symbol; he is a schedule, an expense, and a fact that other people now have to be told about. Crime belongs in the story because crime is what stands nearest to those with no margin, and the film treats that nearness as weather rather than as melodrama.

Freddy runs the gang, Jan is his younger brother, and Cissy moves between them. West German cinema had barely begun looking at its teenagers when this appeared in 1956, and Georg Tressler goes at the subject without a social worker's vocabulary: no diagnosis, no framing lecture, only a set of adolescents with time on their hands and a leader who enjoys the position. The drift toward something serious is gradual, and then it is not gradual. The trouble is domestic before it is criminal, two brothers under one roof, one of whom has already settled what he is, and a girl who understood the arrangement before either of them did. It keeps watching past the point where a cautionary tale would have stopped, and it does not raise its voice.

The West German boom made fortunes quickly, and Rosemarie intends to be paid out of one of them. She has no factory, no capital and no name, only access, which turns out to be the scarce commodity. Her method: the men who run heavy industry talk in bed, and what they say carries a price in France. Rolf Thiele shoots it as a comedy of commerce, in which the industrialists are less seduced than invoiced, and the satire works because every party to the transaction, Rosemarie included, regards it as ordinary business. It took a Golden Globe for best non-English-language film, an odd destination for a picture so unimpressed by the country that produced it. Whatever else the miracle years were, this is them seen from the one position in the economy with a clear view of the participants undressed.

Rudolf Höss commanded Auschwitz, and this is a biography of him in the plainest sense of the word. Theodor Kotulla takes close to two and a half hours over the life, and the length is the argument: an atrocity can be shown in ten minutes, but a career needs time, postings, promotions, paperwork, the years in between. Germany, 1977. The German title files it as one German life among others. The film borrows a form usually reserved for men an audience is invited to admire, hands it to someone it was never built for, and then declines to editorialize. The discomfort does not come from what is depicted. It comes from the calm of the chronology, one appointment after the next, and from how much of the whole undertaking turns out on inspection to have been administration.

Benjamín writes his love letters, they fail, and so he proceeds to the next idea available to him, which is abduction. He is an aging bachelor who lives with his sister. Natividad is young, and nobody has consulted her. The film is filed as a comedy and Carlos Carrera does not flinch from the label, so what follows is built like farce, with a household to manage, a story to keep straight, and people at the door who have to be told something plausible. Nothing about the setup is presented as charming, and the timing stays comic all the way through anyway. The interest lies in how the laughter keeps grazing the thing underneath it: one man's loneliness has become an event in somebody else's life. The comedy never quite lets itself off the hook.

He goes under in 1971 and comes back up twenty years later, into a country that has finished the arguments he was in the middle of. Lauro fell asleep young, holding a young man's picture of what was coming, and he wakes into a Mexico where that picture is period detail and the people who kept him alive have their own nineties to get through. Gabriel Retes plays it as comedy, the only register that fits, because nothing in the situation is tragic exactly. It is badly timed. A man is being asked to take in at one go what everyone around him absorbed year by year, and the film is best on the small friction of that: how people talk now, what things cost, what nobody bothers to explain any more. The future arrives on schedule and belongs to somebody else.
